column2: Write down ten reasons you want to be wealthy, then pick the three most important ones to focus your efforts. Source: A Dog Called Money.
A container labeled with a specific goal where you deposit saved money to fund a single wish. Source: A Dog Called Money.
A collection of photos representing your goals used to visualize success and transform vague wishes into strong desires. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Daily practice of imagining you already possess your goals, which helps you spot opportunities you would otherwise miss. Source: A Dog Called Money.
A notebook where you record at least five personal achievements every day to build self-confidence and belief in your abilities. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Focus on solving a problem for others to find profitable opportunities and create value. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Concentrate your energy on things you already know, can do, and currently possess instead of focusing on what you lack. Source: A Dog Called Money.
When you decide to take action on an idea, you must start within 72 hours, or you will likely never do it. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Destroy all credit cards because the ease of use often leads people to spend more than they would with cash. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Pay the lowest possible monthly installment on loans to ensure you have enough remaining cash to live and continue saving. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Apply half of your non-living expenses to debt repayment and the other half to savings for your 'goose.' Source: A Dog Called Money.
Keep a note in your wallet asking 'Is this really necessary?' to curb impulsive spending at the point of purchase. Source: A Dog Called Money.
The goose represents your capital, and the golden eggs represent interest; you must save enough principal so you can live off the interest without spending the capital. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Allocate 50% of income to long-term savings (the Goose), 40% to goal-oriented savings (Dream Pots), and 10% for personal spending. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Ensure that your primary 'Goose' capital is invested in secure locations where it is protected from total loss. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Select investments that provide significant interest or 'golden eggs,' which typically involves long-term stock market participation. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Choose investment vehicles that are easy to understand and simple to manage. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Divide 72 by your annual interest rate to determine how many years it will take for your money to double. Source: A Dog Called Money.
Divide 72 by the annual inflation rate to find out how many years it will take for your money's value to decrease by half. Source: A Dog Called Money.
An investment where many people pool money for experts to invest in at least 20 different companies to spread out risk. Source: A Dog Called Money.
